## Last week, in one slide

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**A neuron** multiplies each answer by a weight, adds a bias, and squashes.

**Training** is one loop: guess → how wrong (the loss) → blame each weight (backpropagation) → nudge it: $w \leftarrow w - \eta\,(p-y)\,x$.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**An LLM** is the same machine, answering "which of 200,000 tokens comes next?".

It reads **tokens**, lets them **attend** to each other, and knows only what is in its **context window**.
:::
::::

[Today: what it does with those probabilities — and then data, where the assistant writes the code and you check it.]{.explain}

## [Part 1]{.section-kicker} The model's side {.section-slide background-color="#AF1F25"}

## Last week's table, again

`The ECB left rates` → ?

::: {.bigtable}
| unchanged | steady | at | on | higher |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.62 | 0.15 | 0.10 | 0.08 | 0.05 |
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Bet"}
Ask the same question ten times. How many times does it answer "unchanged"?
:::

[It does not look the answer up. It **picks** from these odds — and the setting that decides how it picks is called **temperature**.]{.explain}

## Temperature reshapes the odds {.clip background-color="#000000"}

<video class="clipvideo" width="1000" height="562" controls muted loop playsinline data-autoplay preload="auto" poster="media/w02_temperature_poster.png"><source src="media/w02_temperature.mp4" type="video/mp4"></video>

## The same five tokens, four temperatures

::: {.bigtable}
| next token | T = 0 | T = 0.5 | T = 1 | T = 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **unchanged** | 1.00 | 0.90 | 0.62 | 0.39 |
| **steady** | 0.00 | 0.05 | 0.15 | 0.19 |
| **at** | 0.00 | 0.02 | 0.10 | 0.16 |
| **on** | 0.00 | 0.01 | 0.08 | 0.14 |
| **higher** | 0.00 | 0.01 | 0.05 | 0.11 |
:::

[**T = 0**: always the top token — the same answer every time. Use it for anything that must be reproducible: extraction, classification, anything an auditor will read. Higher T for ideas.]{.explain}

## So where do invented numbers come from?

::: {.callout-important title="Bet"}
You ask for a company's 2025 revenue. The model gives a precise, wrong figure. Bug, lie, or working as designed?
:::

. . .

**Working as designed.** There is always a most likely next token — even when the fact was never in the training data or the context. It produces the *shape* of a number that would fit, with the same confidence.

[It cannot feel the difference between recalling and inventing. That is your job, all term.]{.explain}

## Write it into the procedure

A process an auditor will read cannot say *"we asked the AI"*. It records:

- the **exact prompt**, versioned like code
- **T = 0**, and the model's **name and version**
- the **input** stored next to the answer

## [Part 2]{.section-kicker} Your tiny LLM, piece 1: the tokenizer {.section-slide background-color="#AF1F25"}

## How a tokenizer is learned

Find the pair of symbols that appears most often. Give it a name. Repeat.

::: {.plain}
| merge | the pair seen most often | times | new piece | text length |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| start | | | | 127 |
| 1 | `a` + `n` | 6 | `an` | 121 |
| 2 | `s` + `_` | 5 | `s_` | 116 |
| 3 | `e` + `_` | 4 | `e_` | 112 |
| 4 | `r` + `a` | 4 | `ra` | 108 |
| 5 | `ra` + `t` | 4 | `rat` | 104 |
| 6 | `rat` + `e` | 4 | `rate` | 100 |
| 7 | `rate` + `s_` | 4 | `rates_` | 96 |
| 8 | `t` + `h` | 3 | `th` | 93 |
:::

[Trained on a text about rates, it learns `rates_` as one piece after seven merges. Trained mostly on English, it learns English pieces — and your Russian costs more.]{.explain}

| day | Bitcoin, $ | S&P 500 (SPY), $ |
|---|---|---|
| Fri 05 Jan | 44,163 | 453.09 |
| Sat 06 Jan | 43,989 | — |
| Sun 07 Jan | 43,943 | — |
| Mon 08 Jan | 46,971 | 459.56 |
| Tue 09 Jan | 46,140 | 458.86 |
| Wed 10 Jan | 46,628 | 461.46 |
| Thu 11 Jan | 46,369 | 461.26 |
| Fri 12 Jan | 42,853 | 461.57 |
| Sat 13 Jan | 42,842 | — |
| Sun 14 Jan | 41,796 | — |
| Mon 15 Jan | 42,512 | — |
| Tue 16 Jan | 43,155 | 459.88 |
:::

[The week the US approved spot Bitcoin ETFs. Bitcoin: 12 prices. The stock market: 7 — weekends, and Monday 15 January was a US holiday.]{.explain}

## Four verbs cover most of data work

::: {.bigtable}
| verb | in Excel | in pandas | on our ten days |
|---|---|---|---|
| **filter** | AutoFilter | `df[df.SPY.notna()]` | keep the days the stock market traded |
| **derive** | a formula column | `df.pct_change()` | daily returns |
| **aggregate** | a pivot table | `df.std()` | one volatility number |
| **join** | VLOOKUP | `a.join(b)` | Bitcoin next to the S&P 500 |
:::

[The assistant writes all four faster than you. Your job is to know what the result should look like before you see it.]{.explain}

## A return, by hand

$$\text{return} = \frac{\text{price today}}{\text{price yesterday}} - 1$$

Monday 8 January, Bitcoin: 46,971 / 43,943 − 1 = **+6.9%**

## After every join, three checks

1. **rows before and after** — `len(a)`, `len(b)`, `len(joined)`
2. **missing values** — `joined.isna().sum()`
3. **one row from the middle** — read it

[The calendar is a modelling decision, not a cleaning step. The assistant always makes it — silently.]{.explain}

## [Part 5]{.section-kicker} Units, snapshots, privacy {.section-slide background-color="#AF1F25"}

## A number without a unit

Three daily returns, written in percent: **1.2, −0.8, 0.5**.

::: {.bigtable}
| compounded as | calculation | result |
|---|---|---|
| percent → decimals first | 1.012 × 0.992 × 1.005 − 1 | **+0.89%** |
| read as decimals by mistake | 2.2 × 0.2 × 1.5 − 1 | **−34%** |
:::

[No error, no warning. The code cannot see units; they live in the documentation, and in your head.]{.explain}

## A number without a snapshot is an anecdote

Every number in today's slides comes from one file:

`btc_spy_2022-01-01_2026-09-18.csv` — 1,722 rows, 2022-01-01 to 2026-09-18.

- **save the data** behind every reported number, with the date in the name
- **pin the versions** of your libraries
- **set the seed** wherever randomness enters

[The test: can someone else, on another machine, get your number? If it needs you in the room, it is not a result yet.]{.explain}

## Nothing confidential goes into an AI tool {.statement}

[Not client names, not unpublished figures, not personal data — not even "just to check the formatting".]{.muted}
